1.pericope_label: Righteous art thou, O Lord, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously? Thou hast planted them, yea, they have taken root: they grow, yea, they bring forth fruit: thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins. But thou, O Lord, knowest me: pull them out like sheep for the slaughter. How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott work the grammar and the text: the fidelity phrase attaches to the heart and marks its relation to God, prepare is better rendered devote, and the closing boast carries a variant reading.

Gill and Calvin both set God's righteousness first as a fixed principle, then split on the prophet himself: Gill grants a real temptation resisted, Calvin denies any shaking and reads the complaint as indignation aimed past a deaf people.
Clarke and Wesley keep the difficulty personal and practical, vice in affluence against piety in poverty, ways just but dark, and want the sinners pulled out so the land may be relieved.
Henry treats the confession of God's righteousness as armour put on before the argument begins, and narrows the prosperous to hypocrites.

debates.question: Was the prophet himself shaken by the prosperity of the wicked?

positions.position: Yes, he stood under a real temptation and had to steady himself before arguing.
He was not accusing but seeking satisfaction: the ways are just, only dark.
No, the address to God is a device of indignation, spoken past a deaf people.
Hypocrites, who have God on their lips and nowhere else.
The conspirators of the preceding chapter.
Vice in affluence, taken generally.
Yes, every good thing even of the wicked comes from God, who fixed the bounds of their settlement.
The words are the prophet's distrust speaking: they flourish so that one would think God had planted them.

outliers.claim: Records a variant behind the older Greek in which the closing boast is not that the enemies will outlive the prophet but that God does not see their ways.
Turns the suffering of innocent cattle and birds into an argument from the lesser to the greater: if God has long punished beasts that have no fault, those whose fault it is cannot be spared.

themes: Righteous art thou, O Lord, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?
Thou hast planted them, yea, they have taken root: they grow, yea, they bring forth fruit: thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins.
But thou, O Lord, knowest me: thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart toward thee: pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter.

How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein? the beasts are consumed, and the birds; because they said, He shall not see our last end.

5.pericope_label: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan? For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee: believe them not, though they speak fair words unto thee.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take both halves of the answer as proverbs contrasting a smaller task with a greater, and Ellicott refuses to decide between the flood and the jungle of Jordan for want of data.

Gill identifies the brethren with the men of Anathoth; Calvin reports the reading that makes God himself the horseman and rejects it, holding that the prophet spoke from divine fervour and needed no checking.

Clarke and Wesley read the verse as a warning of worse to come, Wesley setting Anathoth against the capital and Clarke venturing an identification of the footmen and horses with actual national armies.

debates.question: Is the answer a rebuke of the prophet or a preparation for worse?

positions.position: A rebuke of his impatience.
A warning of greater dangers ahead rather than a reproof.
Not a rebuke at all: he spoke from divine fervour and needed no checking.

debates.question: What do the footmen and the horses stand for?

positions.position: The men of Anathoth against the king, court and priests of the capital.
Actual armies, infantry nations against Chaldean cavalry, though the words stay proverbial.
A general contrast of a smaller trial with a greater in the prophet's own office.

debates.question: What is the swelling of Jordan?

positions.position: The river overflowing its banks at harvest.
The flood driving lions and beasts from the thickets to ravage the country.
Undecidable: the phrase may mean the flood or the pride of the jungle, and there are no data for deciding.

debates.question: Who are the brethren that dealt treacherously?

positions.position: The men of Anathoth, his own townsmen and fellow priests.
Actual kin of his own father's house.
Both his town and his own family.

outliers.claim: Suggests that the saying about a prophet having no honour in his own country and his own house probably had its origin in Jeremiah's experience here.
Observes that to raise a cry after a man who has already turned his back and declined the fight is the mark of a settled hatred rather than of ordinary enmity.

themes: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?

For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee: believe them not, though they speak fair words unto thee.

7.pericope_label: I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies. Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it. Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour. Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch defend the passage against those who sever it, while Ellicott confesses the join is unclear and grounds the speckled bird in observed bird life, objecting to the word pastors as too gentle for the men meant.

Gill presses the speckled bird toward a bird stained with blood and reads the forsaken house in two fulfilments; Calvin widens the house to the whole land and takes speckled to mean wild rather than variegated.
Clarke makes the forsaking a covenant term and the plumage borrowed from the nations whose rites were adopted; Wesley reads the heritage as the whole people and states the bird habit plainly.
Henry has God driven from his own palace by their pollution of it, the beloved of his soul returning him hatred for his love.

debates.question: How far does the forsaken house reach?

positions.position: The temple itself, in two fulfilments.
The temple as God's polluted palace, with the people cast out of his protection.
The whole land and people, since the country was reckoned God's habitation on the temple's account.
A bird stained with blood, emblem of a people who shed the blood of prophets.
A bird in borrowed plumage: the nations whose rites were adopted come to reclaim their own.
An uncommon vulture mobbed by birds of another kind, taken from observed bird life.
A wild bird of the wood, set against the tame creatures that keep to their folds.

debates.question: Who are the many pastors that destroyed the vineyard?

positions.position: Heathen princes, the Chaldean king and his generals.
The whole succession of invading nations.
Nomad herdsmen breaking the fence, the figure chosen for its note of systematic plan.
Shepherds set in antithesis to the shepherd God would have gone on being.

debates.question: Does this oracle belong where it stands?

positions.position: The join is unclear; the chapter may be fragments written at intervals and later arranged.
It does: the views that sever it rest on a wrong conception of the passage.

outliers.claim: Reads the forsaking of the house in two fulfilments, the second when Christ took his leave of the temple and a voice was heard within it before the city fell.
Objects to the word pastors itself, whose modern spiritual associations sit badly on men who are reckless and destructive.

themes: I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it.
Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour.
Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.

11.pericope_label: They have made it desolate, and being desolate it mourneth unto me; the whole land is made desolate, because no man layeth it to heart. The spoilers are come upon all high places through the wilderness: for the sword of the Lord shall devour from the one end of the land even to the other end of the land: no flesh shall have peace. They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, but shall not profit.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the threefold desolate as a wail, takes the verb as impersonal, corrects the tense of the sowing, and limits the loss of peace by the context to the offenders of Judah.

Gill takes the high places for fortified strongholds and the sowing for the Egyptian alliance; Calvin makes every individual enemy a master of the land, reads the high places as upland pasture, and extends the loss of peace to all without exception.

Clarke makes the neglect of the judgments the wonder of the passage and diagnoses its cause; Wesley refuses to let God be the subject of the desolating verb and reads the failure to consider as itself a cause of judgment.

positions.position: Impersonal: one has made it desolate, that is, it is made desolate.
The Chaldean king as instrumental cause, or the people and rulers as the meritorious one.
Every individual enemy severally, not the united army only.

debates.question: What are the high places the spoilers come upon?

positions.position: The bare treeless heights chosen for idolatrous sanctuaries.
The strong and fortified places that could not withstand the invaders.
Upland pasture set against the level country, so that no hidden recess is safe.

debates.question: What was sown, and what has failed?

positions.position: The people's own schemes, the alliance sought with Egypt, which proved thorns.
Their projects and counsels generally, none of which can prosper.
Already failed: have reaped thorns and profited nothing, a proverbial saying.

debates.question: How wide is the sentence that no flesh shall have peace?

positions.position: Limited by the context to the offenders of the cities of Judah.
All without exception, rich and poor, countryman and citizen.

outliers.claim: Hears the threefold repetition of desolate as a sound before it is a statement: the Hebrew word, so uttered, must have come out as a wail of lamentation.
Diagnoses the failure to lay the judgments to heart as a settled habit of mind: they think such things come in the course of events.

themes: They have made it desolate, and being desolate it mourneth unto me; the whole land is made desolate, because no man layeth it to heart.
The spoilers are come upon all high places through the wilderness: for the sword of the Lord shall devour from the one end of the land even to the other end of the land: no flesh shall have peace.
They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, but shall not profit: and they shall be ashamed of your revenues because of the fierce anger of the Lord.

14.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord against all mine evil neighbours, that touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit; Behold, I will pluck them out of their land, and pluck out the house of Judah from among them. And it shall come to pass, after that I have plucked them out I will return, and have compassion on them, and will bring them again, every man to his heritage. If they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The Lord liveth; then shall they be built in the midst of my people.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the oath as a chief utterance of religious confession and call the promise Messianic; Ellicott marks the asymmetry of the two pluckings and hears the prophet's own commission in the closing verb.

Gill names the neighbouring nations and turns the condition toward the church of his own day; Calvin extends the mercy to the heathen and finds the faithful's favour doubled by the salvation of their enemies.

Clarke severs the closing oracle, illustrates the scourging of the scourger, and finds the conversion of the Gentiles here; Wesley keeps sword and restoration together and reads the condition as leaving idolatry for the living God.

Henry lays the charge that they were evil neighbours first in debauching Israel and now in desolating her, and holds it just with God to make those the instruments of our trouble whom we made instruments of our sin.

debates.question: Who are the evil neighbours, and on what ground are they God's?

positions.position: Nations lying close to the land where God's people dwelt, evil because they so often distressed it.
Neighbours to his church, so that what is done against her he takes as done against himself.
Those who rejoiced in Judah's fall and struck her in her weakness.
All the neighbouring nations that united to desolate Judea.

debates.question: Does the closing oracle belong to this chapter?

positions.position: No: a different discourse, dated to the seventh or eighth year of Jehoiakim.
Others sever the preceding strophe instead, taking it for a lament over plundering already suffered.

debates.question: Who receives the compassion promised after the plucking?

positions.position: The evil neighbours as well as Judah, though less signally, and from their own land rather than from exile.
Both, and the salvation of their enemies doubles God's favour to the faithful.
The nations too, some abjuring idols so that Jew and Gentile form one church.
Them as well: the sword and captivity first, then a fetching out of it.

debates.question: What does learning the ways of my people require?

positions.position: Adopting the worship of the LORD, an oath being a chief utterance of religious confession.
Reverent and righteous acknowledgment rather than hypocritical form.
What God commanded, not what the people actually practised.
Attendance on word and ordinances, and a hearkening to gospel ministers.

outliers.claim: Illustrates the scourging of the scourger by the practice of making a condemned felon the county hangman while he is still himself under sentence of death.
Hears in the verb of the last verse the prophet's own commission, the very word rendered root out when he was called.

themes: Thus saith the Lord against all mine evil neighbours, that touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit; Behold, I will pluck them out of their land, and pluck out the house of Judah from among them.
And it shall come to pass, after that I have plucked them out I will return, and have compassion on them, and will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.

And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The Lord liveth; as they taught my people to swear by Baal; then shall they be built in the midst of my people.
But if they will not obey, I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation, saith the Lord.
